briefing.opening: Good day. Welcome to the Climate Briefing for November 20, 2026.

sections.title: 🔴 KMA's 7th Climate Scenario Warnings and Setbacks in Global Climate Stocktaking
sections.content: According to the IPCC 7th global climate change scenario projections produced and released by the Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA), if high greenhouse gas emissions persist, temperatures could rise by up to 3.6°C globally and up to 3.8°C in East Asia by the late 21st century [1, 2, 4, 7]. However, as the preparation of the UN climate change report intended to guide the global climate response faces disruptions and delays, leading scientists are increasingly concerned about waning momentum for mitigation [3, 100]. This is highlighted as a serious threat to the international community's collective response framework amid unfolding climate disasters, such as intensifying wildfires in Southeast Asia driven by El Niño and climate change [99, 108, 126].

sections.title: 🌍 Approaching Conclusion, COP31 Sparks Controversy over Removal of 'Fossil Fuel Phaseout' from Draft Text
sections.content: As the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) taking place in Antalya, Türkiye, enters its final stretch, negotiations are experiencing severe turmoil [5, 114, 129]. The draft agreement released in the final stage has ignited fierce backlash, as all language regarding fossil fuels—the primary driver of the climate crisis—has been excised, and climate finance targets for developing nations have been omitted [13, 119, 130, 138]. While there are moves to fill the void left by fossil fuel reduction with 'electrification' and calls from businesses to accelerate electrification, skepticism over the summit's overall effectiveness is growing [11, 17, 35, 117]. Regarding demands from African nations for additional climate finance, negotiations also remain deadlocked as European nations insist on prioritizing the utilization of previously committed funds [101, 137].

sections.title: ⚠️ Carbon Emissions Surge Amid Big Tech's AI Expansion and Challenges for Korea's Energy Transition
sections.content: The downside of advanced technology expansion has surfaced as Meta's aggressive buildout of artificial intelligence (AI) capital expenditures and data centers triggered a 45% surge in greenhouse gas emissions, prompting a review of its original 'Net Zero by 2030' target [47, 52, 53]. In tandem, the International Energy Agency (IEA) pointed out that South Korea's energy import dependence is among the highest in the world, strongly recommending an expansion of renewable energy [66, 84]. Domestically, however, expanding infrastructure on the ground is struggling, as evidenced by the Saemangeum 30MW renewable energy project entering a third re-tender after consecutive failed bids to select an operator [74, 82, 83, 93, 97].

sections.title: 🌱 Domestic Local Governments Secure Renewable Energy Budgets and Drive Preemptive Carbon Neutrality Innovations
sections.content: Domestically, tangible achievements in proactive carbon neutrality and renewable energy deployment are materializing across local governments. The Jeonnam-Gwangju region secured 27.5 billion KRW in national subsidies for renewable energy deployment—including convergence support projects—the largest in the country, providing strong momentum for large-scale rollout projects [58, 62, 73, 86]. In addition, Gunsan City is pursuing institutional innovation by overhauling its greenhouse gas mitigation policy from post-implementation management to a 'preemptive prevention' framework that evaluates emissions right from the project planning stage [25, 49, 51]. Concurrently, municipalities such as Sangju, Geoje, and Seosan were selected as top-performing local governments in the Carbon Neutrality Points Scheme and related competitions, demonstrating strong grassroots implementation capabilities [28, 31, 44, 46].

briefing.closing: Amid climate crisis warnings and the rising emissions burden driven by technological expansion, actionable mitigation agreements and regional-level energy transition efforts are becoming more critical than ever. This concludes today's Climate Briefing.
